title: Lowest Common Ancestor
summary: Finding the lowest common ancestor in a general tree, a BST, and with parent pointers — the ancestor question that shows up disguised in a dozen tree problems.

slides.markdown:
The **lowest common ancestor (LCA)** of two nodes is the deepest node that has both as descendants (a node counts as its own ancestor by the usual convention). It sounds like a single well-defined problem, but the right algorithm depends entirely on what structure you're given: a general binary tree, a BST (which adds ordering you can exploit), or a tree with parent pointers (which turns it into a different problem entirely).

LCA also shows up as a hidden building block inside other problems — computing the distance between two nodes, or the LCA of more than two nodes — which is why it's worth mastering as its own topic rather than only as a one-off question.

slides.sectionTitle: Recursive LCA in a general binary tree
slides.subTitle: The "found in both subtrees" signal
slides.markdown:
In a general binary tree (no ordering to exploit), the approach is: recursively search both subtrees for the two target nodes. If one target is found in the left subtree and the other in the right subtree, the **current node** is the LCA — it's the point where their paths from the root diverge. If both targets are found in the same subtree, the LCA must be somewhere deeper in that subtree, so the answer bubbles up from there instead.

The signal that makes this work: each recursive call returns "did I find either target node in my subtree (and if so, which one, or a special marker if both)" — that returned signal is what the parent uses to decide whether it's the divergence point.

slides.sectionTitle: LCA of a binary tree in one recursive pass
slides.subTitle: No parent pointers needed
slides.markdown:
```python
def lowest_common_ancestor(root, p, q):
    if not root or root is p or root is q:
        return root
    left = lowest_common_ancestor(root.left, p, q)
    right = lowest_common_ancestor(root.right, p, q)
    if left and right:
        return root       # p and q found on different sides — this is the split point
    return left or right  # both found on the same side, or neither found
```

O(n) time (worst case visits every node), O(h) space for the recursion stack. Note this returns `root` itself immediately if `root is p or root is q` — one target being an ancestor of the other is a valid case, and the LCA is then simply that ancestor node itself.

slides.subTitle: Using the ordering property to skip recursing into both sides
slides.markdown:
A BST's ordering invariant makes LCA much cheaper: at any node, if both p and q are smaller than the current node's value, the LCA must be in the left subtree (both targets are to the left, so nothing on the right matters). If both are larger, it's in the right subtree. The moment they're **not** both on the same side — one is smaller or equal, the other larger or equal — the current node is the split point, and therefore the LCA.

This turns an O(n)-worst-case general-tree search into an O(h) walk, since at every step you only ever need to look at **one** direction, never both — exactly the same divide-and-conquer idea that makes BST search itself O(h) instead of O(n).

slides.subTitle: In O(height) with no extra space
Turning it into a linked-list-intersection problem
slides.markdown:
If each node has a pointer to its parent, LCA transforms into a completely different problem in disguise: walking from p up to the root, and from q up to the root, are each just linked-list traversals — and the LCA is exactly the **first node these two "lists" have in common**, which is the linked-list intersection problem from the `linked-lists` group, solved the identical way.

The two-pointer alignment trick applies directly: walk one pointer up from p and one up from q; whenever a pointer reaches the root (the "end" of its list), redirect it to start walking up from the *other* target instead. Both pointers traverse the same total distance before meeting, so they arrive at the LCA simultaneously — no need to compute either node's depth upfront.

slides.sectionTitle: Assuming both nodes exist in the tree
slides.subTitle: LCA breaks silently if one node is missing
slides.markdown:
The standard general-tree LCA algorithm (checking `root is p or root is q`, combining left/right results) **assumes both p and q actually exist somewhere in the tree**. If one of them doesn't, the algorithm doesn't error — it silently returns a plausible-looking but wrong answer, typically whichever single target it did find, mistaking "found one of the two" for "found their LCA."

This matters because the assumption is easy to forget under interview pressure, and a version of the problem that explicitly allows a missing node needs a genuinely different algorithm — one that returns a count or boolean confirming *both* targets were actually found, only returning a real LCA answer once that's confirmed, rather than optimistically returning early. Stating this assumption out loud ("this assumes both nodes are guaranteed to be in the tree") before presenting the standard solution is worth doing proactively.

slides.sectionTitle: General-tree LCA vs BST LCA vs parent-pointer LCA
slides.subTitle: Picking the right one from the input shape
slides.markdown:
| Input shape | Right algorithm | Complexity |
|---|---|---|
| General binary tree, no extra pointers | recursive found-in-both-subtrees | O(n) time, O(h) space |
| BST | ordering-based single-direction walk | O(h) time, O(1) space (iterative) |
| Any tree, with parent pointers | linked-list-intersection style two-pointer walk | O(h) time, O(1) space |

All three answer the identical question — the deepest common ancestor — but the fastest available algorithm depends entirely on what extra structure the input provides. Reaching for the general O(n) algorithm on a BST (ignoring the ordering) or on a tree with parent pointers (ignoring the shortcut) both work correctly but leave a real, testable performance improvement on the table.

slides.subTitle: Distance between two nodes, and LCA of more than two
slides.markdown:
Once LCA is solved, two related problems fall out almost for free. **Distance between two nodes**: find their LCA, then the distance is (depth of p - depth of LCA) + (depth of q - depth of LCA) — the sum of each node's distance up to the shared ancestor, since the shortest path between any two tree nodes always routes through their LCA.

**LCA of more than two nodes**: the general-tree recursive algorithm generalizes directly — instead of checking for exactly two targets, check whether the current node's subtree contains **any** of the target set, and combine results the same way; a node found in more than one child's subtree (or found in one child's subtree while also being a target itself) is the split point. Recognizing LCA as a reusable primitive, rather than a single isolated question, is what lets these variations get solved quickly rather than from scratch.
